rewrites.summary:
In Amritsar — the spiritual centre of the region's dominant faith — Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade at the Rose Garden after "mounting resistance" from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, the faith's highest temporal authority; organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason for cancelling the annual event (Washington Blade, 23 April 2025). No other Punjab-specific law, ordinance or institution affecting trans people appears in the audited sources for this record.

For a trans visitor the documented signal is institutional, not criminal: no statute here targets trans people, but an organised religious authority compelled the cancellation of the region's annual public trans assembly, and the event simply did not happen. Public visibility in Amritsar therefore carries a documented precedent of organised religious opposition, and the absence of any recorded state intervention to preserve the event is part of that record.

No local statute criminalising trans people is documented.

The suppression record is institutional rather than criminal: organised religious authority ended the region's main public trans assembly, and no intervention preserving it was recorded.

rewrites.summary:
Kerala holds a constituted Transgender Welfare Board — one of the 12 states/UTs reported to the federal parliament in December 2021 as having set one up under the national trans-protection rules (PIB) — and its law-enforcement machinery is measurably engaged: the state registered 2 of the 7 national cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 and 4 of the 11 recorded in 2023, among the highest sub-national totals in those years (queerbeat data report, 30 January 2026).

That activity should be read with the source's own caveat: national recording is sparse (20 cases across 2019–23) because of police registration bias, against survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence (2025 Transgender Health study, n=4,964). Registered cases therefore evidence a system that at least accepts complaints, not rarity of violence. No Kerala-specific restriction is documented; for a visitor the picture is one of institutional recognition machinery in a state where such machinery exists and is used.
rewrites.blindSummary:
A south-western region has a constituted transgender welfare board (listed among 12 sub-national units so reported in a December 2021 federal parliamentary reply) and registered 2 of 7 national cases under the country's trans-protection law in 2021 and 4 of 11 in 2023.

The audit source reads such low counts as police under-registration (20 cases nationally 2019–23; 2025 survey prevalence 27.2% physical, 22.3% sexual). Complaint machinery exists and is used; no local restriction is documented.
blindSourceSummaries: Data-journalism report (30 Jan 2026): only 20 cases nationwide 2019–2023 under the country's trans-protection act — 7 in 2021 (2 each in two states, including this one, and 3 in a third) and 11 in 2023 (7 in one state, 4 in this one); scarcity attributed to registration bias against 2025 survey prevalence data.
Official federal parliamentary reply (8 Dec 2021): 12 states/union territories have constituted transgender welfare boards under the 2020 federal rules; this region is among them.
rewrites.notes: Dropped first-policy and scholarship claims (unsupported here); kept board + case-count facts.

rewrites.summary:
Assam appears in national crime records with 2 of the 7 cases registered under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021, and none in the 2023 tally (queerbeat data report, 30 January 2026) — which itself cautions that national counts are tiny (20 cases 2019–23) because of police registration bias, with 2025 survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence. Recorded cases prove the complaint system is reachable, not that violence is uncommon.

In the December 2021 federal reply listing the 12 states/UTs that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards (PIB), Assam is not among them — i.e., no state welfare machinery stood in place as of that date. No Assam-specific protective or restrictive statute, ordinance or checkpoint operation is documented in the audited sources; the record supports a thin official-visibility finding balanced against the region-wide caveats, nothing more.

rewrites.summary:
Ceará is the most consistent lethal hotspot for trans and travesti people in Brazil's Northeast: 11 killings in 2024 — the region's highest toll and third nationally (G1, 28 January 2025, on the ANTRA dossier) — and 8 in 2025, tied with Minas Gerais for the highest state total of that year's 80 nationwide (Igbá Agência, 26 January 2026; SBT News). The 34% national drop is not read as improvement by ANTRA's leadership, since violence reappeared as attempted homicides (at least 75) (SBT News).

There is no state-level legal distinction: the federal constitution and penal code apply uniformly. What sets Ceará apart is sustained lethal exposure, and the national victim profile sharpens it for a visibly trans traveller — 97% of victims are travestis and trans women, over half aged 18–29, 70% of those with recorded race are Black, 97% killed in public spaces with most incidents outside capitals. Two consecutive years at the top of the ranking indicate an entrenched environment rather than a statistical blip.
rewrites.blindSummary:
A northeastern state led its region in killings of trans people in 2024 (11, third nationally) and tied for the national top state total in 2025 (8 of 80), in two consecutive annual dossier rankings; the national drop is attributed to violence shifting into attempted homicides (75+), not improvement.

No local legal distinction exists — federal law applies uniformly. The national victim profile (97% travestis/trans women, majority 18–29, 70% Black, public-space killings mostly outside capitals) defines the exposure of a visibly trans traveller.
blindSourceSummaries: Brazilian news portal (28 Jan 2025): this state had the Northeast's highest number of trans-person killings in 2024 — 11, third nationally — per the annual association dossier.

Independent agency (26 Jan 2026): 9th annual dossier — this state tied for the highest 2025 state total (8 of 80 national); Northeast accounted for 38; 70% of identified victims Black; decline attributed to displacement into attempted homicides.

Broadcast news (Jan 2026): 80 killings in 2025 (–34%); 97% of victims travestis/trans women; most 18–29; 67.5% outside capitals; 1,261 killings 2017–2025; Brazil world-leading since 2008; this state in the top tier.
rewrites.notes: Dropped score metadata and per-capita math; moved Black-victim share to national framing.

rewrites.summary:
Paraíba recorded 4 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — mid-pack in the ANTRA dossier's state ranking, alongside Paraná, Rio Grande do Norte and São Paulo — within a national total of 80 that still leads the world for the 16th consecutive year (SBT News, 26 January 2026; CNN Brasil). No Paraíba-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources; the federal framework applies uniformly.

The documented signal is therefore exposure, not law: the dossiers' consistent victim profile — young, Black, poor and Northeastern, 97% travestis and trans women, most killings in public spaces at night and outside state capitals, frequently mis-recorded by authorities — concentrates risk on people who present visibly in public. The state's absolute count doubled the best-recorded small-state figure of the same table's lower rows, and sits inside the region the dossiers identify as Brazil's hardest-hit.
rewrites.blindSummary:
A northeastern state logged 4 killings of trans people in 2025, mid-pack in the annual monitoring dossier, in a country that remains the world's deadliest for trans people for a 16th consecutive year. No local statute or policy specific to trans people is documented; federal law governs uniformly.

The risk documented here is street exposure matching the national victim profile — young, Black, poor, northeastern travestis and trans women killed in public at night, often mis-recorded — not any legal distinction.

National broadcast (Jan 2025): the country leads global trans-murder tallies again (122 in 2024); victims young, Black, poor, northeastern; life expectancy ~35; killings in public, at night, with cruelty, routinely mis-recorded.

rewrites.summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, behind only the two 8-count states in the ANTRA dossier's ranking of that year's 80 national killings (SBT News, 26 January 2026; Valor Internacional). No Pernambuco-specific legal restriction or ordinance was identified in the audited sources; the federal framework applies uniformly.

The dossiers add a geographic caution that cuts against capital-centred assumptions: roughly two-thirds of such killings in Brazil happen in interior cities rather than state capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker (SBT News). A visibly trans visitor in Pernambuco's mid-sized and interior municipalities is therefore in the geography where the recorded danger actually concentrates — alongside a victim profile of young (majority 18–29), overwhelmingly Black (70% of those recorded) travestis and trans women.
rewrites.blindSummary:
A northeastern state recorded 7 killings of trans people in 2025 — second only to the two top states in the annual dossier, of 80 nationally — with no local statute or policy specific to trans people documented.

Because roughly two-thirds of such killings nationally occur outside the capitals in harder-monitored interior cities, the documented danger concentrates in this state's mid-sized and interior public spaces rather than its capital's tourist geography; victims are mainly young Black travestis and trans women.

The documented picture is a high absolute toll diluted by size rather than eliminated by it: the dossiers place the state inside the Northeastern region that accounts for the bulk of national killings, with the consistent victim profile (97% travestis and trans women, majority aged 18–29, 70% Black among racially identified cases, most killings outside state capitals) describing who carries the risk. For a visibly trans visitor the operative fact is persistence — Bahia appears in the top ranked band of consecutive annual dossiers — not any local legal regime.

rewrites.summary:
Maranhão recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — the same count the association dossier logged for it in 2024 — so its position in the ranking's middle-upper band is persistent rather than a one-year spike (SBT News, 26 January 2026; CNN Brasil, 27 January 2025). No Maranhão-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people is documented in the audited sources; federal law applies uniformly.

The national profile the dossiers attach to this state's region — victims young, Black, poor and Northeastern; 97% travestis and trans women; most killings in public places, at night, and outside state capitals where monitoring and policy access are thinner — maps onto Maranhão's place in both tables. The documented risk is structural exposure: two consecutive years of above-median lethal counts in a country that leads the world's tallies, without any local legal change either way.

A northeastern state recorded 5 killings of trans people in both 2024 and 2025 in the annual monitoring dossiers — persistent middle-upper band exposure in a country that leads global tallies — with no local statute or policy specific to trans people documented.

The region-matched victim profile (young, Black, poor travestis and trans women; killings in public, at night, mainly outside the capital where services are thinner) defines the risk as structural rather than legal.

Pará recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, in the middle band of the ANTRA dossier's state ranking of that year's 80 national killings (SBT News, 26 January 2026). The second audited source lists the 2024 worst-hit states without naming this state, so its 2024 position cannot be fixed from the record.

What the dossiers do document bears directly on a vast Amazonian state: roughly two-thirds to 68% of such killings nationally occur in interior cities outside the capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker, and victims are overwhelmingly young Black travestis and trans women killed in public places. For a trans visitor travelling beyond the main metropolitan area, the least-monitored geography is precisely where the recorded killings sit.

rewrites.summary:
Alagoas recorded 6 killings of trans and travesti people in 2024 — among the elevated small-state totals in that year's ANTRA dossier table (CNN Brasil, 27 January 2025) — and 2 in 2025 (SBT News, 26 January 2026). No Alagoas-specific legal restriction or enforcement finding is documented; federal law applies uniformly.

The swing between consecutive dossiers on a small population is itself the finding: at these denominators a couple of cases moves a state's position sharply, which is why the monitoring body cautions that falling national counts reflect violence shifting into attempted homicides and persistent under-recording (misclassification of victims' gender identity degrades the data) rather than improving safety. The victim profile the dossiers attach to this region — young, Black, poor, Northeastern, killed in public places at night — places risk wherever a visibly trans person is in public, in a state inside the country's hardest-hit region.

Risk tracks the regional victim profile — young, Black, poor travestis and trans women, killed publicly at night — within the country's worst-affected region and interior-city geography.
